forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
question: What happens when the Ballerina’s graceful triple time has to coexist with her partner’s heavier movement?
intro: The rival puppet’s room exchanges Petrushka’s agitation for weighty repetition, a toy-like dance and borrowed waltzes. The score’s “Moor” is an exoticised theatrical stereotype: its music should not be mistaken for a portrait of an actual African or Muslim musical tradition.

cues.title: Weight before melody
cues.text: Abrupt gestures introduce the room before the main low wind tune settles in. Compare this orchestral weight with the exposed lines of Petrushka’s room: the rival puppet receives a different musical gait, not simply a louder version of the same theme.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 78–79, rehearsals 62–64, gives the ferocious introduction and low transition. Boundaries at 0:12 and 0:26 precede the quieter, darker 0:25–0:40 interval. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An emphatically low centre
cues.text: The introduction settles into a low-centred passage before the main dance. Listen for how a heavy bass and measured punctuation establish physical character even before the melody becomes the principal focus.
cues.evidence: Score p. 79, rehearsal 64, gives low strings, tuba, bassoon and percussion. The analysis measures low spectral centroids at 0:25–0:40; it does not itself identify those instruments. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A stereotype, not ethnography
cues.text: The original stage directions give the Moor a decorated room, a scimitar and a coconut he mistakes for a supernatural object. These are the ballet’s exoticising props and character conventions, not evidence about a real culture or its music.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer, Summary and original-version structure, rehearsals 62–68. The critical distinction is editorial; the props and actions are documented. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: A tune doubled in octaves
cues.text: The principal low melody is assigned to clarinet and bass clarinet in octaves. Repeated percussion and a relatively steady accompaniment make it feel planted, in contrast to Petrushka’s more interruptive, exposed gestures.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 79–80, rehearsals 65–66, documents the octave doubling and accompaniment. The report shows a stable pitch profile across 0:50–1:35 and withdrawal around 1:40; this cue describes the extended dance, not a fresh tune entrance at 1:48. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A gesture interrupts the tread
cues.text: The dance’s steadier surface is not unbroken. A short, much stronger passage interrupts it before the level falls again; keep the underlying low-centred character in mind through the sudden theatrical gesture.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-moor.txt: boundaries at 2:06, 2:10 and 2:24 bracket the strongest five-second window at 2:10, followed by much lower level at 2:25–2:35. No specific coconut blow is inferred from the measurement. Scenario source: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka.

cues.title: The ballerina brings a toy
cues.text: The scenario has the Ballerina enter carrying a toy trumpet. In the original orchestration her little solo is given to a cornet with military drum: a stage object and the orchestral instrument representing it need not have the same name.
cues.evidence: The entrance and toy trumpet are specified before rehearsal 69; score p. 83 labels the solo “Pistoni I” and the accompaniment “Tamburo militare”. This is contextual preparation, not an entrance timed at 3:00. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

cues.title: A tiny public performance
cues.text: Cornet and military drum reduce the Ballerina’s dance to a strikingly small ensemble. Listen to the exposed melodic line and its regular accompaniment: the delicacy comes from the scale of the forces as much as from the tune.
cues.evidence: Score p. 83, rehearsal 69, leaves the cornet and drum alone for the opening of the dance. The 3:14 boundary sharply raises brightness after 3:10, and the 3:15–3:35 interval remains comparatively quiet. Passage placement is approximate. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna inside the puppet theatre
cues.text: For the pair’s waltz, Stravinsky borrowed melodies from Joseph Lanner. Familiar ballroom grace becomes theatrical material: it can make the Ballerina sound elegant while exposing the ungainliness of her partner’s accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner’s programme note identifies two Lanner waltzes and describes the competing duple accompaniment. This does not assign an exact borrowed-tune entry to the cue time. https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911

cues.title: Count three against two
cues.text: In the waltz sequence, keep counting the melody’s triple movement while attending to the partner’s heavier accompaniment. The mismatch is deliberately left in place: the instruments can share a passage without agreeing on the same pattern of steps.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 84–88, rehearsals 71–75, contrasts waltz melody with the returning low accompaniment; Larner explicitly describes the metre conflict. The report’s changes at 4:50 and 5:04 support internal changes within this extended sequence, not a bar-exact duple entry. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Elegance acquires weight
cues.text: The waltz passage grows much stronger before receding. Follow the balance across the phrase: changes of orchestral weight can turn a seemingly graceful dance into a contest between its participants.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-moor.txt: relative level rises from −22.6 dB at 4:50 to roughly −12 dB at 5:00–5:20, then retreats by 5:35–5:40. This is a measured dynamic contour; the theatrical interpretation follows https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka.

cues.title: The low character returns
cues.text: The earlier low-centred material returns within the dance sequence. The waltz has not erased the rival puppet’s musical identity; familiar colours and melodic contours can interrupt the ballroom surface from inside it.
cues.evidence: The score’s rehearsal 75 recalls the earlier character material. The report’s strongest change at 5:44 leads to the E♭/B♭/E pitch profile previously found at 0:50–1:35. This supports a broad return, not a machine-derived key or exact tune alignment. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The duet cannot continue
cues.text: Petrushka’s intervention breaks the dance apart. Muted brass calls and sharper exchanges replace the pair’s attempted continuity; the scene becomes a quarrel rather than allowing the waltz to find a comfortable conclusion.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 89–91, rehearsals 76–78, gives the appearance, muted brass and ensuing quarrel. The 6:24 change precedes increased brightness at 6:30–6:40; exact character entrances remain unaligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Driven out of the room
cues.text: The closing passage drives towards a brief crest and then withdraws. The scenario has the Moor chase Petrushka away: the private rivalry is left unresolved before the ballet returns to the public fair.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-moor.txt: relative level rises strongly at 7:05–7:15, then drops at 7:20 before the 443.6-second endpoint. The chase and curtain are documented at rehearsals 79–81: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka.

transitions.title: Violent gestures settle into a heavy tread
transitions.how: Feroce gestures and string weight give way to a slower, lower-centred span. Bassoon and low accompaniment prepare the clarinet-and-bass-clarinet melody. The low register persists while the texture becomes more regular, so the new dance grows from the introduction’s physical weight without preserving its agitation.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 78–79, rehearsals 62–65. The 0:26 boundary leads to low brightness through 0:40; a further boundary at 0:48 separates the settling passage from the sustained dance. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: A solo display replaces the low tread
transitions.how: The Ballerina’s entrance redirects attention from the room’s low, weighty accompaniment to cornet and military drum. Allegro begins her dance with only those two parts, making the change of theatrical focus unusually explicit. The cornet’s register and exposed articulation matter more here than any connecting modulation.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 82–83, rehearsals 68–69. At 3:14 the report detects a change; brightness rises from 785 Hz at 3:10 to 2318 Hz at 3:15 while the level remains low. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: A cadenza opens the ballroom miniature
transitions.how: The small solo dance expands briefly, then a flute cadenza leads to the waltz. Flute, cornet and bassoon give the new melody and accompaniment a light initial scoring. The triple-time dance will soon have to accommodate the partner’s incompatible tread; the join establishes elegance before that mismatch becomes the point.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 83–84, rehearsals 70–72. The report drops in relative level and brightness at 3:55–4:05; this places the lighter opening approximately, without aligning the flute’s final note. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: A third voice breaks the dance
transitions.how: Muted trumpets and cornets, stopped horns and trombone writing interrupt the dancing pair. The score passes from Meno mosso into renewed activity as Petrushka appears. Instead of completing the waltz, the orchestra exchanges its continuing dance texture for short, opposed gestures that carry the quarrel.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 89–91, rehearsals 76–78. The 6:24 report boundary separates the returned low material from a brighter, more articulated stretch at 6:30–6:40. The appearance itself is not bar-aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 78–95, rehearsals 62–81. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-moor.txt. Both harps share one stage position; active groups vary within the indicated passage.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
